title: Machines of Borrowed Grace
subtitle: Where a Language Model Gets Its Meaning, and Where Its Makers Get Theirs
author: Anonymous
lead: Whether a machine can think is a question about what it is for anything to mean something.
Language models now do work that used to take a mind. What are they, where do their words get their meaning, and what are the companies building them standing on?
description: This book asks what large language models actually are, where the meaning in their sentences comes from, and what the companies building them are relying on. It treats the machines as signs from end to end, numbers and tokens that mean something only because people trained them and people read them. It walks through ordinary examples like a word, a sum, a thermostat, and a sieve to show why the models can outperform most of us at coding, writing, and problem-solving without possessing a mind of their own. The first half stays close to the machine: how a sign comes to mean anything, whether a machine can think or feel, whether it can improve itself into understanding, and what would count as proof that it had. The second half turns to the people who make and sell the models, looking at the visions they offer of a future shaped by AI and the unstated assumptions those visions rest on.

The writing is plain and conversational, starting from everyday observations and building outward in the manner of Herbert McCabe explaining Aquinas. It draws mainly on Aristotle and Aquinas, with substantial help from Wittgenstein and more recent philosophers such as James Ross, while keeping technical claims about language models and their training tied to public sources. The author is explicit about working from a classical Christian frame, and the book moves from the philosophy of mind into questions of moral alignment, human dignity, and what a healed or flourishing human life would look like once AI is widespread.

Readers curious about AI beyond benchmark scores, especially those who wonder whether the technology requires any revision of older ideas about thought, meaning, or human nature, will find a sustained and accessible treatment here. It is less a technical survey of current models than a philosophical map of the territory the models occupy, written for anyone who wants to think through the claims that the machine understands, that alignment is the hard part, or that AI will deliver the good life, without needing prior training in either philosophy or machine learning.

title: Mere Catholicity
subtitle: What has been believed everywhere, always, and by all
author: Anonymous
lead: For the layman, it is all about 1054. The great wound in Christendom is not the changes of the last century. It is the Great Schism of 1054, when East and West tore apart, and so much of the later tearing follows from it.
description: For the layman, it is all about 1054. The great wound in Christendom is not the changes of the last century. It is the Great Schism of 1054, when East and West tore apart, and so much of the later tearing follows from it. The faith of the first thousand years is the ground the ancient churches still share. What each side defined after the tear it defined alone, and what a part defines alone cannot bind the whole until the whole comes to confess it. This book is a call to walk back, past every later rupture, to that first faith, and it is addressed to every house that still keeps a part of it, Roman, Orthodox, Anglican, Lutheran, Presbyterian.

For the theologian, the thesis is this. A council binds when the whole Body comes to confess the faith it defined, and binding by act alone never existed in the conciliar age, for the Body has been torn since 251 and reception across the open tears is attested wherever it has been checked. The church that refused Ephesus confesses, in Babai, the one Christ Ephesus defined. The churches that refused Chalcedon confess, in Severus, the faith it guarded. Measured by that record, the definitions added since the great schisms, Vatican I and the Marian dogmas on one side, the Palamite councils on the other, stand not yet received, never condemned, and the book denies both communions the same thing, the identification of the whole with a part. It keeps Newman's method while declining his authority, claims Ratzinger's Graz formula as lineage, quotes the ex sese clause rather than paraphrasing it and stands under its anathema, grades every disputed act of both millennia in an appendix, and lets its own rules cut against its own comfort, usury the hardest case, the veil left binding unless a retraction is shown. It closes with a proposal in Zoghby's genre made mutual, synodal professions by which each communion holds its post-schism definitions as patrimony rather than exacting them as conditions of communion.

And if this is true, then Tolkien and Lewis, the Roman Catholic and the Anglican who between them taught the last century's laymen to love the permanent things, are not divided now as they were at every altar on earth, and may well be smoking their pipes side by side in heaven, having a laugh with Luther, who swore he would sooner drink the blood of Christ with the papists than mere wine with the fanatics. And Dostoevsky is there too, the Orthodox among them, who always suspected heaven would be more crowded than the experts allowed. The hope of this confession is not more complicated than that.
